overview: Pelorosaurus (meaning 'monstrous lizard') was a large titanosauriform sauropod from the Early Cretaceous (approximately 145–110 million years ago) of England, UK, and possibly France. Fossils assigned to Pelorosaurus include material from the Wealden Group and Lower Greensand of southern England. Estimated at up to approximately 24–25 metres in length, it was one of the largest dinosaurs known from the Early Cretaceous of Europe. It was a quadrupedal herbivore.

Named by Gideon Mantell in 1850, Pelorosaurus is one of the earliest-named sauropods and has a notoriously complex taxonomic history: numerous species from England and other countries were assigned to the genus over more than a century, most of which have since been reassigned or declared nomina dubia. The first-named species, P. conybeari, is now considered a junior synonym of Cetiosaurus brevis. The genus is placed within Titanosauriformes (PBDB and NHM both confirm this). Despite the nomenclatural confusion, 'Pelorosaurus' material remains scientifically important as among the earliest evidence for large-bodied titanosauriforms in western Europe.

articles.title: Discovery and Naming
articles.body: Pelorosaurus conybeari was named by Gideon Mantell in 1850, making it one of the oldest names applied to any sauropod. Mantell based it on a humerus and vertebral material from Sussex, England. The name 'monstrous lizard' reflects nineteenth-century appreciation of the animal's enormous size. The genus name Pelorosaurus was among the first to be given to any sauropod dinosaur, predating widespread understanding of sauropod biology.

articles.title: Taxonomic Complexity
articles.body: More than a dozen species have been assigned to Pelorosaurus over the past 170 years, from England, Portugal, the United States and elsewhere. The vast majority of these assignments have since been rejected or reassigned to other genera. P. conybeari itself is now a junior synonym of Cetiosaurus brevis. This species-level instability makes Pelorosaurus a cautionary example of how historical 'wastebasket' taxa can accumulate unrelated material.

articles.title: Early Cretaceous European Sauropods
articles.body: The Early Cretaceous of western Europe was a time of reduced terrestrial faunal diversity compared to the Late Jurassic. Sauropods were less abundant but still present, and material assigned to Pelorosaurus documents the persistence of large titanosauriforms into the Hauterivian and Aptian of Britain. These animals would have inhabited the seasonal subtropical lowlands of the European archipelago.

articles.title: Scientific Legacy
articles.body: Despite its taxonomic difficulties, Pelorosaurus material from England has contributed to understanding the anatomy of early titanosauriforms. The humerus from the type specimen, described by Mantell, was one of the first sauropod bones to be formally illustrated and discussed, making it historically significant in the development of vertebrate palaeontology as a discipline.

record.description: Pelorosaurus conybeari is a historically important but taxonomically difficult English sauropod name based on Early Cretaceous Wealden material. Its type concept involves a humerus and historically associated caudal vertebrae; many species once placed in Pelorosaurus do not belong there.
facts: The name has been applied inconsistently since the nineteenth century.
Pelorosaurus becklesii was removed to the separate genus Haestasaurus in a modern revision.
A precise body plan or family-level placement for P. conybeari is not secure.
